title: Good for the hive
hookLine: what isn't good for the hive isn't good for the bee (Meditations 6.54)

lines: BAD FOR ALL, THEN FOR EACH.
cards: A shared kitchen: an apartment, an office, a dorm. One person leaves their dishes in the sink because it's quicker, just this once. Then another does.
By Friday nobody can make a sandwich, including the person who started it. What was good for one of them turned out bad for all of them, and then bad for each of them.
Marcus wrote a one-line entry about this, and it's about bees.

teach.b: Here's the whole entry, Book Six, section fifty-four, in George Long's translation: "That which is not good for the swarm, neither is it good for the bee." One line.
Marcus's Greek word can mean the swarm or the hive: the whole buzzing community. No single bee makes the honey.

teach.h: A HIVE THAT FLIES IN SMALL PIECES.
teach.b: What we call a bee is really a hive that happens to fly around in small pieces. The Stoics believed people were like that.
We're made to work together, Marcus says early in the book, the way hands and feet and eyelids are. So he couldn't picture a good that was only his.
If a choice helped Marcus and hurt Rome, it wasn't really good for Marcus either.

teach.h: NO HARM TO THE CITY, NONE TO YOU.
teach.b: In Book Five he flips it around: what doesn't harm the city doesn't harm the citizen. So if something annoys you but hurts no one, maybe it isn't really harm. The line cuts two ways.
It's a check on selfishness: before the shortcut, ask what it does to the hive. And it's a comfort: you're not a lone bee trying to make honey by yourself.
You belong to something bigger, a household, a street, a team, the whole human family, and your good is tied up with theirs.
Of course, Marcus isn't saying the hive is always right, or that one person should be sacrificed for the group. He's saying a real good can't be yours alone. Your line: the hive.

how: The Stoics taught that human beings are made for community, and many readers of Marcus use this line as a quick test for their choices: is this good for the people around me?

o: a sudden crowd that rushes in to attack
a flock of birds flying south together
the whole hive, a community working as one

games.q: what goes with what — tap the pairs.
p: what doesn't harm it doesn't harm you

s: Marcus says what's bad for the swarm can still be good for the bee
that which is not good for the swarm, neither is it good for the bee.
Marcus says one person should always be sacrificed for the group
he says a real good can't be yours alone, not that the group is always right.
the Stoics believed people are made for each other
Marcus compares us to hands, feet and eyelids working together.

games.q: you're in a shared kitchen, in a hurry. leaving your dish in the sink would save you two minutes. what does Marcus's bee do?
o: leave it; one dish won't matter.
wash it; what's bad for the hive is bad for the bee.
leave a note blaming someone else.
games.why: for Marcus, a shortcut that harms the hive isn't really good for you either.

practice: Picture your hive: the people you live with, or near, or work beside, one by one.

Then think of one small thing that would make the shared space better, emptying the dishwasher, taking out the trash, a kind note on the fridge, a call to a parent, and hold it in mind as a gift to the hive.

wordCard.voice: Swarm. Marcus's word for the whole hive: what isn't good for the swarm isn't good for the bee either. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: a swarm of bees, or a hive: the whole community. Marcus's word in this entry.

carryVoice: Your line: the hive. No bee makes honey on its own. Day two hundred one, done.
